{{lang|es|chiapaneco}} | government_type = }} The '''Zapatista territories'''{{cite news |url=https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2011/1/1/zapatistas-the-war-with-no-breath |title=Zapatistas: The war with no breath? |first=Chris |last=Arsenault |work=[[Al Jazeera English]] |date=2011-01-01 }}{{cite web |url=https://www.internationaleonline.org/contributions/echoes-of-zapatismo-outside-chiapas/ |title=Echoes of Zapatismo outside Chiapas |first=Alessandra |last=Pomarico |work=Internationale |date=2022-11-19 }}{{cite journal |url=https://academic.oup.com/isagsq/article/4/3/ksae072/7824740 |title=A World of Many Walks? Zapatista World Ordering between Center and Margins |first=Christine |last=Unrau |journal=[[Global Studies Quarterly]] |volume=4 |issue=3 |date=2024-10-17 |at=ksae072 |doi=10.1093/isagsq/ksae072 |doi-access=free }} are a ''de facto'' [[autonomous territory|autonomous region]] controlled or partially controlled by [[neozapatismo|neo-Zapatista]] support bases in [[Chiapas]], [[Mexico]]. They have existed since the [[Zapatista uprising]] in 1994 and are part of the wider [[Chiapas conflict]].{{Cite web |last=Reyes Godelmann |first=Iker |date=30 July 2014 |title=The Zapatista Movement: The Fight for Indigenous Rights in Mexico |url=https://www.internationalaffairs.org.au/news-item/the-zapatista-movement-the-fight-for-indigenous-rights-in-mexico/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250117232611/https://www.internationalaffairs.org.au/news-item/the-zapatista-movement-the-fight-for-indigenous-rights-in-mexico/ |archive-date=17 January 2025 |access-date= |publisher=[[Australian Institute of International Affairs]]}} From 1994 to 2003, the Zapatista territories were structured as regional community centers called Aguascalientes. In 2003, the Aguascalientes were replaced by Centers of Autonomous Resistance and Zapatista Rebellion (CRAREZ),{{cite web |last=Moisés |first=Subcomandante Insurgente |date=17 August 2019 |title=Communique from the EZLN's CCRI-CG And, We Broke the Siege |url=https://enlacezapatista.ezln.org.mx/2019/08/20/communique-from-the-ezlns-ccri-cg-and-we-broke-the-siege/ |access-date=8 November 2023 |work=[[Zapatista Army of National Liberation|Enlace Zapatista]]}} a term coined in 2019, which consisted of ''Caracoles'' as community centers, over local formations (until 2023) as the Rebel Zapatista Autonomous Municipalities (MAREZ) governed by Councils of Good Government ([[Spanish language|Spanish]]: ''{{lang|es-MX|Juntas de Buen Gobierno}}'').{{cite web |author=Subcomandante Insurgente Marcos |date=July 2003 |title=Chiapas: La treceava estela |url=https://palabra.ezln.org.mx/comunicados/2003/2003_07_e.htm |website=Cartas y comunicados del EZLN}} In 2023, after increased cartel violence, the EZLN announced the dissolution of the CRAREZ and its sub-formations, replacing them with Local Autonomous Governments (GAL) within local Zapatista Autonomous Government Collectives (CGAZ) and regional Assemblies of Collectives of Zapatista Autonomous Governments (ACGAZ).{{Cite web |author=Insurgent Subcommander Moisés |date=2023-11-13 |title=Ninth Part: The new structure of Zapastista Autonomy |url=https://enlacezapatista.ezln.org.mx/2023/11/13/ninth-part-the-new-structure-of-zapastista-autonomy/ |access-date=2023-11-13 |website=Enlace Zapatista}} Despite attempts at negotiation with the [[Mexican Government|Mexican government]] which resulted in the [[San Andrés Accords]] in 1996, the region's autonomy remains unrecognized by it.{{Cite news|last=Villegas|first=Paulina|date=2017-08-26|title=In a Mexico 'Tired of Violence,' Zapatista Rebels Venture Into Politics|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/08/26/world/americas/mexico-zapatista-subcommander-marcos.html|access-date=2020-05-07|issn=0362-4331}} The [[Zapatista Army of National Liberation]] (EZLN) does not hold formal political power in Zapatista governance. According to its constitution, no commander or member of the ''Clandestine Revolutionary Indigenous Committee'' may take positions of authority or government in these spaces.{{cite book |author=Gloria Muñóz Ramírez |title=20 y 10 el fuego y la palabra. |year=2003 |publisher=Revista Rebeldía y Demos, Desarrollo de Medios, S.A. de C.V. La Jornada Ediciones.}} == History == {{Expand section|date=March 2025}} === Zapatista uprising === On 1 January 1994, thousands of EZLN members occupied towns and cities in Chiapas, burning down police stations, occupying government buildings, and skirmishing with the Mexican army. The EZLN demanded "work, land, housing, food, health care, education, independence, freedom, democracy, justice, and peace" in their communities.{{Cite book|last=Muñóz Ramírez|first=Gloria|year=2008|title=The Fire and the Word: A History of the Zapatista Movement|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5fkMAQAAMAAJ|pages=22|translator-first1=Laura|translator-last1=Carlsen|translator-first2=Alejandro|translator-last2=Reyes Arias|publisher=[[City Lights Bookstore|City Lights]]|isbn=978-0-87286-488-7|lccn=2007052477}} The Zapatistas seized over a million acres from large landowners during their revolution.{{Cite book|last1=Grubačić|first1=Andrej|author-link1=Andrej Grubačić|last2=O'Hearn|first2=Denis|author-link2=Denis O'Hearn|year=2016|chapter=Zapatistas|title=Living at the Edges of Capitalism: Adventures in Exile and Mutual Aid|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=raowDwAAQBAJ|publisher=[[University of California Press]]|isbn=9780520287303|lccn=2015036704|jstor=10.1525/j.ctv1xxx8z|page=129}} === Reorganization in 2003 === In 2003, the Aguascalientes were replaced by Centers of Autonomous Resistance and Zapatista Rebellion (CRAREZ), a term coined in 2019, which consisted of ''Caracoles'' as community centers, over local formations (until 2023) as the Rebel Zapatista Autonomous Municipalities (MAREZ) governed by Councils of Good Government ([[Spanish language|Spanish]]: ''{{lang|es-MX|Juntas de Buen Gobierno}}''). === COVID-19 pandemic === {{See also|COVID-19 pandemic in Mexico}} COVID triggered a decline in the Zapatista movement owing to inconsistent responses around cooperating with the Mexican government to distribute the vaccine.{{Cite web |title=The difficult art of sustaining alternative governance: the case of the EZLN |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/action/cookieAbsent |access-date=2026-04-06 |website=www.tandfonline.com |doi=10.1080/21622671.2025.2583055}} === Dissolution of MAREZ in 2023 === In early November 2023, a communique signed by Subcomandante Moises announced the dissolution of the Rebel Zapatista Autonomous Municipalities,{{cite web |last=Clemente |first=Édgar H. |date=6 November 2023 |title=Mexico's Zapatista rebel movement says it is dissolving its 'autonomous municipalities' |url=https://apnews.com/article/mexico-indigenous-zapatista-rebels-violence-04006895dc4bd430b4b957d459551a12 |access-date=8 November 2023 |work=[[Associated Press]]}}{{Cite web |last=Henríquez |first=Elio |date=2023-11-05 |title=Anuncia EZLN desaparición de sus municipios autónomos |url=https://www.jornada.com.mx/noticia/2023/11/05/estados/anuncia-el-ezln-desaparicion-de-sus-municipios-autonomos-1703 |access-date=2023-11-09 |website=[[La Jornada]] |language=es}}{{Cite web |last=Flores |first=Miguel |date=2023-11-07 |title=Así fue como el EZLN perdió el control de municipios autónomos en Chiapas frente al CJNG y el Cártel de Sinaloa |url=https://www.infobae.com/mexico/2023/11/07/asi-fue-como-el-ezln-perdio-el-control-de-municipios-autonomos-en-chiapas-frente-al-cjng-y-el-cartel-de-sinaloa/ |access-date=2023-11-09 |website=[[Infobae]] |language=es}}{{Cite web |last=Ferri |first=Pablo |date=2023-11-06 |title=El EZLN anuncia la desaparición de su estructura civil: "Las ciudades de Chiapas están en caos" |url=https://elpais.com/mexico/2023-11-06/el-ezln-anuncia-la-desaparicion-de-su-estructura-civil-las-ciudades-de-chiapas-estan-en-caos.html |access-date=2023-11-09 |website=[[El País]] |language=es}} along with their Councils of Good Government. The announcement declared that, effective immediately, all positions and documents related to the MAREZ would be considered invalid. The statement clarified that the Caracoles (Zapatista community centres) would continue providing their services to locals, but would be "closed to outsiders". Although he did not describe specific reasons for the dissolution, Moises cited rising cartel violence along the [[Guatemala–Mexico border]], where many of its municipalities are located. The state of [[Chiapas]] had already been experiencing a rise in [[people smuggling]], [[drug trafficking]] and open conflict between the [[Sinaloa Cartel]] and the [[Jalisco New Generation Cartel]]. In September 2021, the EZLN had described the situation in the state as a "[[civil war]]". The Zapatistas reported that the cartels, which they linked with the Mexican government, had carried out "road blockades, robberies, kidnappings, extortion, forced recruitment, [and] shootouts" in the region. The statement described the cities of Chiapas as being in "complete chaos", and that many (including [[San Cristóbal de las Casas]], [[Comitán]], [[Las Margaritas, Chiapas|Las Margaritas]] and [[Palenque, Chiapas|Palenque]]) were controlled by the cartels. They also reported that the [[Mexican Army]] and [[National Guard (Mexico)|National Guard]], which had deployed thousands of troops to the region, had not combatted criminal violence; they claimed that the Mexican state's troops were only there to prevent [[illegal immigration to the United States]]. According to the statement, the decision to dissolve the MAREZ had been discussed for months prior to the announcement. It has been speculated that the decision had been taken due to the then-upcoming [[2024 Mexican general election]]. According to Mexican anthropologist Gaspar Morquecho, the Zapatistas had also become "increasingly isolated", cutting ties with other organisations. Morquecho claimed this had caused many in the younger generation to leave the Zapatista municipalities, in order to seek work or education. Moises promised that future statements would clarify the reasons for the decision, as well as details on the restructuring of "Zapatista autonomy". The statement also stated the Zapatistas' intention to celebrate the 30th anniversary of their uprising, inviting people to come, while also warning that Chiapas was no longer safe. In the middle of the month, EZLN issued a declaration that announced the new structure for the autonomous region. The new structure is more decentralized and would replace the previously dissolved Municipalities, allowing the base communities to better unite and act.{{Cite web |last=CounterVortex |date=2023-11-22 |title=THE NEW ZAPATISTA AUTONOMY |url=https://countervortex.org/the-new-zapatista-autonomy/ |access-date=2024-09-11 |website=CounterVortex |language=en-US}} == Distribution == Since 2003, the Rebel Zapatista Autonomous Municipalities (MAREZ) coordinated in very small groups called ''{{lang|es-MX|caracoles}}'' (English: "snails" or "seashells"). Before that, the Neo-Zapatistas used the title of Aguascalientes after the site of the EZLN-organized National Democratic Convention on 8 August 1994;{{Cite web|url=https://itzcuintli.tripod.com/b.html|title=Los Aguascalientes: Centros Culturales en el Corazón de la Selva Lacandona y en las montañas y rincones zapatistas.|website=itzcuintli rebelde|access-date=2018-09-14}} this name alluded to the [[Convention of Aguascalientes]] during the [[Mexican Revolution]] where [[Emiliano Zapata]] and other leaders met in 1914 and Zapata made an alliance with [[Francisco Villa]]. {| class="wikitable" |+Distribution of Rebel Zapatista Autonomous Municipalities (MAREZ) locations{{cite journal|last1=Hidalgo|first1=Onésimo|last2=Castro Soto|first2=Gustavo|title=Cambios en el EZLN|journal=Chiapas al Día|series=Boletín de CIEPAC|date=2003|location=San Cristóbal de las Casas}}{{cite magazine|last=Oikonomakis|first=Leonidas|date=2019-08-19|url=https://roarmag.org/essays/zapatistas-announce-major-expansion-of-autonomous-territories/|title=Zapatistas announce major expansion of autonomous territories|magazine=[[ROAR Magazine]]|issn=2468-1695|access-date=8 November 2023}} |- ! Here the people rule and the government obeys." Bottom: "North Zone. Council of Good Government. [[Weapons trafficking|Trafficking in weapons]], [[planting]] of drugs, [[Recreational drug use|drug use]], [[alcoholic beverage]]s, and illegal sales of [[wood]] are strictly prohibited. No to the destruction of [[nature]]." Federal Highway 307, [[Chiapas]].]] [[File:Zapatistas Territory sign in Chiapas, Mexico.jpg|thumb|right|300px|Zapatistas Territory sign in Chiapas, Mexico]] Within the MAREZ, [[popular assembly|popular assemblies]] each consisted of around 300 families in which anyone over the age of twelve could participate in decision-making. These assemblies strove to reach a [[Consensus decision-making|consensus]], but were willing to fall back to a [[majority vote]]. The communities formed a federation with other communities to create an autonomous municipality, which formed further [[Federalism#Federalism and localism in anarchist political theory|federations]] with other municipalities to create a region.{{cite magazine|first=Andrew|last=Flood|title=The Zapatistas, anarchism and 'Direct democracy'|url=https://anarchism.pageabode.com/the-zapatistas-anarchism-and-direct-democracy/|magazine=[[Anarcho-Syndicalist Review]]|issue=27|year=1999|issn=1069-1995}} Each community had three main administrative structures: (1) the ''commissariat'', in charge of day-to-day administration; (2) the ''council for land control'', which dealt with forestry and disputes with neighboring communities; and (3) the ''agencia'', a community police agency.{{Cite book|last=Barmeyer|first=Niels|year=2009|chapter=Who is Running the Show? The Workings of Zapatista Government|title=Developing Zapatista Autonomy: Conflict and NGO Involvement in Rebel Chiapas|url=https://archive.org/details/developingzapati0000barm|url-access=limited|publisher=[[University of New Mexico Press]]|page=89|isbn=978-0-8263-4584-4|lccn=2008045276}} == Public services == After the dissolution of the MAREZ, Subcomandante Moises said in an official statement that the Caracoles (Zapatista community centres) would continue providing their services to locals, but would be "closed to outsiders". === Education === The Zapatistas run hundreds of schools with thousands of teachers. They are modeled around the principles of [[democratic education]] in which students and communities collectively decide on school curriculum and students are not graded.{{Cite book|last=Zibechi|first=Raúl|year=2012|title=Territories in Resistance: A Cartography of Latin American Social Movements|publisher=[[AK Press]]|isbn=978-1-84935-107-2|lccn=2012937110|pages=132}} === Healthcare === The Zapatistas maintain a [[Universal health care|universal healthcare]] service which is provided free of charge. However, patients still have to pay for medications to cover restocking costs.{{Cite web|title=Health and Autonomy: the case of Chiapas|url=https://www.who.int/social_determinants/resources/csdh_media/autonomy_mexico_2007_en.pdf|first=J.H.|last=Cuevas|date=March 2007|website=World Health Organization|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211123184551/https://www.who.int/social_determinants/resources/csdh_media/autonomy_mexico_2007_en.pdf|archive-date=2021-11-23}} The Zapatistas built two new hospitals and 18 health clinics in the region by the mid-1990s. One 2014 study indicated the following achievements in Zapatista healthcare: * In 2005, 84.2% of Zapatista children were fully vaccinated, while that figure stood at 74.8% in pro-government communities.{{Cite web|last=Castellanos|first=Laura|date=2014-01-04|title=El suicidio ronda en San Andrés|url=https://archivo.eluniversal.com.mx/nacion-mexico/2014/impreso/el-suicidio-ronda-en-san-andrs-212031.html|access-date=2020-06-16|website=[[El Universal (Mexico City)|El Universal]]|language=es}} * In regions where there were previously significantly high rates of death during childbirth, there has now been a period of eight years or more where no maternal deaths have been recorded. * The manufacture and consumption of alcohol has been banned, which is directly linked to the reduction in many illnesses and infections including ulcers, cirrhosis, malnutrition, and surgical wounds.{{Cite book|date=October 2014|last=Warfield|first=Cian|title=Understanding Zapatista Autonomy: An Analysis of Healthcare and Education|url=https://www.academia.edu/33163010|language=en}} Banning the consumption of alcohol was a collective decision. Nayely, a Zapatista representative, stated that alcohol is "not good for one's health, and just wastes money".{{Cite web |first=Alex|last=Contreras Baspineiro|date=2004-05-08|title=The Zapatistas Reject the War on Drugs |url=https://www.narconews.com/Issue33/article971.html |access-date=2022-12-24 |website=[[Narco News]]}} According to one account of [[Oventic]] from 2016:
In Oventic, there was a small yet seemingly fully-functional medical clinic, which appeared to offer basic healthcare. A sign on the door said general consultations, gynecology, optometry and laboratory services were all available five days a week. Emergency services were available 24 hours, seven days a week. They appeared to have a shiny new ambulance at their disposal. Other services offered a few days a week included dentistry and ultrasounds.{{Cite web|first=Ryan|last=Mallett-Outtrim|date=2016-08-13|url=https://links.org.au/two-decades-glimpse-inside-zapatistas-capital-oventic|title=Two decades on: A glimpse inside the Zapatista's capital, Oventic|website=Links: International Journal of Socialist Renewal|access-date=2023-05-01}}
=== Water === Many Zapatista communities are in rural areas with little access to running water. Projects were undertaken to supply Zapatista communities with fresh water. In one case, [[Roberto Arenas]], a small [[Tzeltal people|Tzeltal]] community, built its own water service with the help of solidarity activists. Such projects were coordinated democratically. An account by Ramor Ryan noted:{{Cite book|last=Ryan|first=Ramor|year=2011|title=Zapatista Spring: Anatomy of a Rebel Water Project & the Lessons of International Solidarity|url=https://archive.org/details/zapatistaspringa0000ryan/|url-access=limited|publisher=[[AK Press]]|isbn=978-1-84935-072-3|lccn=2011925323}}{{rp|10}} {{Blockquote|text=The good government committee of the autonomous municipality refer the case to their elected water commission and the options are weighed. The commission consults various parties including the local EZLN commander and clandestine committee members, and so, in the end, after the issue has been bandied around what seems like half the inhabitants of this particular region of the jungle, the community of Roberto Arenas is notified about the eligibility of their request. It’s a process similar to what happens anywhere in the world at a local council level, except for one significant difference: the state authorities have no involvement whatsoever; this is an autonomous process overseen by the communities’ people. There is no separation between who is governed and who is governing—they are one and the same.}} Ryan described the process of finishing the water project:{{r|Ramor|p=179}} {{Blockquote|text=We’re getting lots of little bits and pieces done, fine tuning this and that. Helping people construct their family tap stands, digging here and there, testing the pressure, tightening valves. A group of women come together during the morning to put together a tap stand for the collective clothes washing area. We earmark a bag of cement—the very last one—for the later construction of a large concrete washbasin. The day is punctuated by minor moments of crisis—people coming up and saying that the water isn’t arriving to their house—but it is usually just a blocked pipe or a faulty connection. Really, the system is almost flawless and works perfectly fine; it’s been an exemplary project.}} ==See also== {{div col|colwidth=20em}} *[[Cherán]] *[[Chiapas Media Project]] *[[Chiapas conflict]] *[[Democratic Autonomous Administration of North and East Syria]] *[[FEJUVE]] *[[Libertarian socialism]] *[[Marinaleda]] *[[Permanent autonomous zones]] *[[Revolutionary Catalonia]] *[[Villa de Zaachila|Zaachila]] *[[Zapaturismo]] *[[Zapatista Army of National Liberation]] {{div col end}} == References == {{Reflist}} ==Bibliography== ===Books=== {{refbegin|2}} *{{Cite book|last=Barmeyer|first=Niels|year=2009|chapter=Who is Running the Show? extract:
The Zapatista territories are a de facto autonomous region controlled or partially controlled by neo-Zapatista support bases in Chiapas, Mexico. They have existed since the Zapatista uprising in 1994 and are part of the wider Chiapas conflict.
From 1994 to 2003, the Zapatista territories were structured as regional community centers called Aguascalientes. In 2003, the Aguascalientes were replaced by Centers of Autonomous Resistance and Zapatista Rebellion (CRAREZ), a term coined in 2019, which consisted of Caracoles as community centers, over local formations (until 2023) as the Rebel Zapatista Autonomous Municipalities (MAREZ) governed by Councils of Good Government (Spanish: Juntas de Buen Gobierno).
In 2023, after increased cartel violence, the EZLN announced the dissolution of the CRAREZ and its sub-formations, replacing them with Local Autonomous Governments (GAL) within local Zapatista Autonomous Government Collectives (CGAZ) and regional Assemblies of Collectives of Zapatista Autonomous Governments (ACGAZ). Despite attempts at negotiation with the Mexican government which resulted in the San Andrés Accords in 1996, the region's autonomy remains unrecognized by it.
The Zapatista Army of National Liberation (EZLN) does not hold formal political power in Zapatista governance. According to its constitution, no commander or member of the Clandestine Revolutionary Indigenous Committee may take positions of authority or government in these spaces.
